title: Roof condition, skylights and fragile surfaces
audience: Trainee or new worker on the roof soft washing track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to roof condition, skylights and fragile surfaces.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instruction.heading: Why roof condition decides the job
instruction.body: Before anyone thinks about cleaning a roof, the roof itself has to be understood. Its condition decides whether a person can stand on it, where water and chemicals will travel, and which parts of the job must be left alone. Falls through roofs are a serious and well-known cause of injury in construction and trades work. WorkSafe Victoria's 2024 safety alert about a worker who fell from a roof describes a guardrail that came loose from a parapet wall and was found on the ground; the alert does not state the cause, and it says a guardrail may fail where the supporting structure has not been verified. The lesson for a soft-washing worker is that a surface that looks finished can still give way under a person's weight, and that a barrier is only as reliable as the structure behind it. This lesson teaches you to observe the roof, record what you see, separate what you know from what you assume, and stop when the answer is not clear. It does not teach you to walk a roof, judge its structure or sign it off.

instruction.heading: Reading a roof from the ground
instruction.body: Most of the useful information about a roof can be gathered without setting foot on it. Walk the full perimeter of the property where it is safe and lawful to do so, and photograph each roof plane from more than one angle. Look for sheeting that bends between fixings, cracks or chalky patches in tiles or fibre-cement, rust that has perforated metal, lifted or slipped tiles, displaced ridge capping, cracked mortar, and sealant applied in heavy patches as if to stop leaks. On polycarbonate and acrylic rooflights, look for yellowing, crazing, scratches and any sign that the sheet has been walked on. Note roof-mounted equipment, solar arrays, cables, vents, box gutters and penetrations. Write each observation as you saw it, for example 'ridge capping displaced at the north-east end', and keep a separate column for anything you have only inferred, such as 'the sheeting may be thin'. Zoomed photographs help, but a photograph does not show the strength of a material, so any decision on strength stays with a competent person.

instruction.heading: Skylights, rooflights and other openings
instruction.body: A skylight is both an opening and a surface that may not carry a person's weight, and it is one of the most common causes of serious falls through roofs. Treat every skylight, rooflight, penetration and other opening as an exclusion zone until a competent person has confirmed how it is protected. The NSW code of practice for work on roofs, which took effect on 22 May 2026, asks that the risk assessment identify brittle or fragile surfaces, skylights, penetrations and other openings before work begins. Where an opening is found, the code expects steps to stop people walking into it, such as barricades or a restraint system. Any cover should be securely fixed, look distinct from the roof sheeting so that it is not lifted off by mistake, and withstand the concentrated load the code sets, which is at least 2 kN. Those checks belong to the competent person and the duty holder. A worker does not decide that a cover is adequate. Mark each opening on the job plan, and confirm that no cleaning path crosses it.

instruction.heading: Treating unknown surfaces as fragile
instruction.body: The working rule in this course is that every roof material is treated as potentially fragile until a competent person establishes otherwise. That rule is a training position rather than a quoted regulation, and it exists because appearance is a poor guide to strength. Weathered sheeting can look solid and still give way. Older fibre-cement sheets can resemble modern ones and may contain asbestos. Whether the asbestos rules cover roof sheeting is not confirmed by an official source, so the state summary in the asbestos lesson of this course applies. As a working rule in this course, a worker does not disturb suspected fibre-cement and refers it for assessment. A statement that the roof was walked last year, or that the owner has never had a problem, is information to record. It is not an assessment. The question is not whether the roof looks safe. The question is who has assessed it, when, and what they found.

instruction.heading: Height and the control hierarchy
instruction.body: Work at height is the central issue in roof cleaning. Safe Work Australia's guidance on working at heights lists the control options in order: first, eliminate the risk or minimise it, for example by doing the work on the ground or from a solid structure; second, a fall prevention device such as a barrier, scaffold or elevating work platform; third, a work positioning system; and last, a fall arrest system. WorkSafe Victoria's alert sets out a similar sequence in a slightly different order, with passive devices and work positioning ahead of fall arrest, and ladders or administrative controls at the end. The difference matters because the sequence that applies is the one used by the regulator in the state where the job sits, so this lesson does not choose between them. On the threshold, use the official wording for the state where the job sits. SafeWork NSW requires a safe work method statement (SWMS) for work where a person could fall more than 2 metres, and work over 2 metres needs fall-prevention controls; whether the high-risk work rules apply at 2 metres is not confirmed by an official source. In South Australia, from 1 July 2026, construction work that involves a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk construction work. Ask first whether any part of the job can be done from the ground, and record the answer.

instruction.heading: Overhead lines, solar arrays and other electrical hazards
instruction.body: Roofs often carry hazards that are not part of the roof itself. The SafeWork NSW code on work near overhead and underground electric lines (May 2026) says a worker should assume an overhead line is live unless there is an access authority or written documentation from the supply authority. Workers must not measure a line's height directly, and must not use metal tapes to estimate it. For ordinary persons, the code sets a distance of 3.0 metres from lines up to 132,000 V. For conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines, it sets 4.0 metres. Queensland's WorkSafe page also sets a 3-metre exclusion zone for powerlines up to 132 kV, and Energy Safe Victoria sets 3.0 metres as the distance within which work near an overhead distribution line needs permission from the network operator; it does not describe a 3 metre no-go zone. Where a line is closer than these distances, or its position cannot be confirmed, stop and refer the work to the supply authority. Solar arrays are a separate hazard. Energy Safe Victoria's guidance (reviewed 15 April 2025) says that PV DC supply cables may still be live when the power is off, and the Western Australian guide (last updated 26 November 2024) says panels keep generating while the mains is disconnected. Electrical testing, isolation and repair of PV systems need a licensed electrician, and plain panel washing is not stated by the official page to need a licence. The working rule is simple. Treat every panel and cable as live, do not touch or isolate them, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instruction.heading: Recording what you saw and what you did not
instruction.body: A record is useful only if a reader can tell what was seen, when, where, and how much weight to give it. Each entry should carry a date, a location label that matches the job plan, and a photograph reference. Keep three categories apart. Observed means you saw it and can describe it. Inferred means you believe it from indirect evidence, and you say so. Unknown means you cannot see it, or no one has assessed it. A fourth category, determinations, belongs to specialists: whether the roof is structurally sound, whether a sheet is fragile, whether a chemical is compliant, and whether asbestos is present. A worker records these questions and names who must answer them. A line such as 'the roof is in good condition' is a determination presented as an observation. A line such as 'ridge capping lifted at two points, photographs 4 and 5' is an observation that a reader can check.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and hold decisions
instruction.body: A hold means the job does not proceed until a named condition is met, such as written authority from the owner, a competent roof assessment, or confirmation by a licensed person that electrical supply is isolated. A stop-work decision applies when a hazard appears during the job. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if a surface, access point or platform is unstable or uncertain, if weather or light changes conditions, if a skylight or opening is found unprotected, if a person or animal enters an exclusion zone, if live or damaged wiring is seen or suspected, or if the task falls outside your authorisation. A waiting customer, or a belief that the roof was fine last time, is not a reason to continue past any of these points.

instruction.heading: Open points in this draft
instruction.body: Check your state or territory regulator before any work above ground level.

procedure: Request the roof plan, the building's age if known, and any earlier roof assessment, and record anything that is missing.
From a safe position on the ground, walk the perimeter where it is safe and lawful, and photograph each roof plane from several angles.
Mark each roof area on the job pack as observed, inferred or unknown, with a date and location label.
Identify every skylight, rooflight, penetration, opening and solar array, and mark each as an exclusion zone until a competent check is recorded.
Note any overhead line or service cable near the roof, do not measure it, and ask the supply authority if its position or voltage is uncertain.
Apply the height hierarchy and record whether any part of the job can be done from the ground without roof access.
Decide whether the job may proceed. It may not proceed on any roof area that is unknown or held, and it may not proceed without written authority and a competent assessment.
Record the decision, the people told, the open items and the person who must resolve each one before the job is rescheduled.

workedExamples.situation: A brick home has faded polycarbonate skylights, weathered metal sheeting and no record of how the roof was built. The owner asks for a wash this weekend and says a previous contractor walked the roof last year.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not walk the roof, and do not treat the previous visit as an assessment. Photograph each roof plane from the ground, mark the skylights as openings and exclusion zones, and mark the sheeting as unknown for strength. Issue a hold. Tell the owner in writing that the roof needs a competent assessment and that the skylights stay excluded until a protection plan is confirmed. Tell the site controller or supervisor, and record who was told and when. The owner's account of the previous visit goes into the record as information, not as an assessment.

workedExamples.situation: A concrete tile roof has a cracked ridge, a solar array on the north-facing plane, and overhead service cables close to the eave. The customer wants the whole roof finished before the weekend.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which parts of the job are held, and what must be referred?
workedExamples.reasoning: The solar array and the overhead cables are electrical hazards outside this lesson. Treat the array and its cables as live, do not touch them, and refer any electrical question to a licensed electrician or the network operator. Treat the cracked ridge as unknown and as a fall hazard, and hold the ridge work. Assume the service cables are live until the supply authority confirms otherwise, and do not measure them. Because access to every plane is still unassessed, the whole roof is on hold. Record each hold and the person who must confirm it.

workedExamples.situation: During a ground walk, a worker sees rust perforations on a corrugated metal section behind a box gutter. The planned route to reach the gutter runs along the ridge.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What does the worker do with the planned route?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop planning the ridge route. The perforations mean the sheet's strength is unknown, the box gutter is a known fall-through point, and the ridge route passes over material that has not been assessed. Look for an option that avoids roof access. If none exists, the route is held for a competent assessment. Photograph the perforations, mark the route as held, and tell the supervisor. This lesson does not authorise any ladder or roof access to reach the gutter.

equipmentAndPpe: Camera or phone with date and time stamping switched on, and zoom for ground observation.
Paper or digital job pack with a roof plan and columns for observed, inferred and unknown items.
Measuring tape for the ground layout only. Never use it to measure a line or a roof height.
High-visibility clothing, safe enclosed footwear and sun protection for the ground walk.
Hard hat where overhead cables, falling debris or building works are present.
No ladder, scaffold, elevating work platform or roof access equipment is covered by this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Assuming the roof is sound because it looks intact.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat every roof material as potentially fragile until a competent person says otherwise, and record appearance as an observation only.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a previous visit or the owner's word as an assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Record it as information with a date and source, and request a competent assessment.

commonErrors.error: Treating a skylight as a surface that can be walked over.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark every skylight and rooflight as an exclusion zone, and confirm its protection with a competent person.

commonErrors.error: Measuring the height of an overhead line to plan the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Never measure a line. Assume it is live and ask the supply authority.
Describe what was seen on a named plane on a stated date. Leave strength and compliance to the specialists.

commonErrors.error: Continuing past a hold because the customer is waiting.
commonErrors.prevention: A hold stays in force until the named condition is met and recorded.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and authority notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, roof-work authority or height authority, and completing it does not allow anyone to climb onto a roof. Check your state or territory regulator, and obtain your employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level.

Height hierarchy and high-risk threshold: Safe Work Australia's working-at-heights guidance sets a control hierarchy that starts with eliminating the risk. SafeWork NSW requires a SWMS for work where a person could fall more than 2 metres, and work over 2 metres needs fall-prevention controls; whether the high-risk work rules apply at 2 metres is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia's threshold of more than two metres applies from 1 July 2026. Apply the version used by the regulator in the state where the job sits.

NSW roof code scope: The NSW code of practice for work on roofs (cover dated May 2026, commenced 22 May 2026) does not cover residential roofs. Its requirements on risk assessment, skylights, openings and covers apply to commercial and industrial roofs in NSW. The part of the text read in this session lists cleaning of roofing material but does not address gutter cleaning or roof washing, so the NSW position for soft washing is only partly confirmed.

Overhead lines: The SafeWork NSW code on work near overhead and underground electric lines (May 2026) says to assume a line is live unless there is an access authority or written documentation from the supply authority. For ordinary persons it sets 3.0 metres for lines up to 132,000 V, and 4.0 metres for conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines.

Solar (PV) electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar systems or any electrical installation. Treat every panel and cable as live. Electrical testing, isolation and repair of PV systems need a licensed electrician, and plain panel washing is not stated by the official page to need a licence. Refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

Asbestos in older sheeting: Asbestos removal licence rules are set state by state, and the state-by-state summary is in the asbestos lesson of this course. In NSW, removing any amount of friable asbestos, or more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos, needs a licence (SafeWork NSW, Asbestos page, last modified 28 October 2026). Whether the asbestos rules cover roof sheeting is not confirmed by an official source. As a working rule in this course, suspected fibre-cement roof sheets are referred for assessment and are not disturbed. This lesson does not grant an asbestos licence or clearance.

Stop-work rule: Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if a surface, access point or platform is unstable or uncertain, if weather or light changes conditions, if a skylight or opening is found unprotected, if a person or animal enters an exclusion zone, if live or damaged wiring is seen or suspected, or if the task falls outside your authorisation.

qualityStandard: The job plan shows every roof plane, skylight, rooflight, opening, penetration and solar array, each labelled and marked as excluded or held until a competent check is recorded.
Each entry in the record is labelled observed, inferred or unknown, and carries a date, a location label and a photograph reference.
No entry states that a roof, sheet, fixing or cover is sound, compliant, non-fragile or asbestos-free.
Overhead lines and solar arrays are recorded as live, not measured, and referred to the supply authority or a licensed person.
Every hold or stop-work decision names the condition to be met, the person notified and the person who must resolve it.
documentationEvidence: A dated photo set taken from ground level, labelled by roof plane and location, with the original files kept unedited.
An observed, inferred and unknown table for the roof, with the source of each inferred item.
An opening and exclusion register listing each skylight, rooflight, penetration and solar array, its protection status, and the competent person who must check it.
A hold or stop-work record showing the date, the condition, the people notified and the owner of each open item.
summary: Roof condition decides whether anyone can work on a roof, so observe from the ground first and keep what you saw apart from what you inferred.
Treat every roof material as potentially fragile until a competent person says otherwise, and treat every skylight and opening as an exclusion zone.
Overhead lines and solar arrays are electrical hazards this lesson does not cover. Assume they are live, do not measure or touch them, and refer them on.
A hold stays in place until the named condition is met and recorded. Nothing in this lesson is a safety or compliance clearance.

knowledgeChecks.question: A roof has faded polycarbonate skylights and an unknown load capacity. Which action follows the lesson's controlling principle?
options: Assume the sheeting is sound, because the owner says the roof was walked last year.
Treat all roof material as potentially fragile until a competent person establishes otherwise.
Walk the roof but keep off the skylights, because the sheeting looks weathered rather than broken.
Start the wash from the roof edge and stop only if someone falls through.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is an observation rather than a determination?
options: The roof is structurally sound for foot traffic, as the owner's inspection confirmed.
The sheeting is not fragile, so it can be walked on by the crew at the job.
The ridge capping is displaced at two points, shown in photographs 4 and 5.
The chemical is compliant with the site requirements and the rules on the job.

knowledgeChecks.question: A skylight lies in a roof plane you would need to cross. What is the correct response?
options: Cross near its edge, where the frame is strongest and the sheet is supported by the rafters below it.
Mark it as an exclusion zone and ask a competent person to confirm how it is protected before any access is planned.
Tell the owner the skylight is unlikely to break, so the wash can continue on the same plan today.
Remove the skylight so the wash can proceed without any obstruction on the roof plane, then refit it.

knowledgeChecks.question: The height of an overhead service line is unknown. What should happen?
options: Measure the height with a metal tape held at arm's length from the ground under the line and note it.
Assume the line is live, do not measure it, and ask the electricity supply authority before work nearby.
Assume the line is dead because it runs on a timber pole along the street and looks old.
Ask the owner to confirm that the line is safe before the work starts on the roof today.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does the lesson say most of the useful information about a roof is gathered?
options: By climbing onto every roof plane
By standing on the skylights to test them
By asking the neighbour only
Without setting foot on the roof, by walking the perimeter and photographing each roof plane from more than one angle
